channel.title: Researches on Marginalia
channel.description: Recent content in Researches on Marginalia

item.title: The Hungry Mirror: Culture and Unmet Human Need
item.description: Finds good evidence that some cultural use compensates for frustrated needs and that some digital affects are self-reinforcing, but reserves the stronger label “parasitic” for systems shown to benefit from recurrent unresolved need rather than inferring dependence from market size or cultural popularity.

item.title: Intergenerational Extraction in Liberal Democracies
item.description: Finds a real democratic vulnerability to intergenerational burden shifting, but reserves the term extraction for cases where politically advantaged present cohorts improve their lifetime net position by externalizing uncompensated costs to younger or future cohorts.

item.title: Republicans as Moderating Opposition Without a Rival Order
item.description: A current-through-2026 test of the Republican moderating-opposition thesis that finds genuine retrenchment in some mature policy domains but durable Republican replacement or state-building in welfare, taxation, trade, and immigration enforcement.

item.title: Liberalism, Social Disembedding, and Managed Dependency
item.description: Examines how modern liberal-capitalist societies shift dependency from inherited persons and communities toward markets, public administration, credentials, professions, and digital infrastructures, and asks when those systems expand practical freedom versus creating opaque or weakly contestable dependency.

item.title: Conserving a Revolution
item.description: Argues that American conservatism’s real tension is not the mere fact of conserving a revolutionary regime, but the need to rank several conflicting inheritances: colonial constitutional tradition, universal natural rights, republican institutions, unequal historical practices, and later American social traditions.

item.title: Puritan Moral Psychology and the Genealogy of American Progressivism
item.description: Finds real Puritan influence through transformed Protestant reform and later national reception, while rejecting a single uninterrupted genealogy that reduces the heterogeneous and transnational Progressive movement to secularized New England moral psychology.

item.title: Fallen Aristocrats: Status Loss, Elite Conversion, and Political Reaction
item.description: A source-audited comparison of how former hereditary and estate-based elites convert residual prestige, networks, education, and organizational capacity after institutional privilege collapses.

item.title: Judges in the Judicial Process of the United States
item.description: A structured guide to U.S. judges and judicial offices across federal and state systems, including tenure, appointment, elections, powers, and pay.

item.title: Aesthetics for the Maimed
item.description: An intentionally severe essay proposing “liberal gothic” as a bounded label for cultural forms organized around haunted interiority, therapeutic recognition, damaged intimacy, and moralized injury, while testing—and sharply limiting—the stronger claim that contemporary culture deliberately preserves suffering for profit.

item.title: Dead Symbols and their Worship
item.description: An intentionally severe, aphoristic essay arguing that parts of mathematical culture confuse abstraction, difficulty, and proximity to unsolved problems with intellectual strength, while undervaluing synthesis, closure, pedagogy, and completed mastery.

item.title: Liberal Gothic: A Diagnostic Taxonomy
item.description: A bounded diagnostic taxonomy of “liberal gothic” as a proposed mode in which Gothic recurrence, wounded interpretation, and limited mastery converge, with explicit exclusion tests and cross-media boundary cases.

item.title: What Knowledge Was Worth: Office, Patronage, and Technical Power in Europe, c.1100–1850
item.description: A source-audited history of how European institutions converted different forms of knowledge into office, jurisdiction, property, patronage, clients, corporate recognition, and technical-state careers from c.1100 to c.1850. Rejects a simple law-to-mathematics succession in favor of multiple, overlapping prestige exchange rates.

item.title: Brickmaking: History, Materials, Processes, and Production Planning
item.description: Covers brickmaking from raw-material preparation through forming, drying, firing, testing, environmental control, production-scale planning, and current kiln-decarbonization work, while distinguishing stable process knowledge from time-sensitive standards and project economics.

item.title: Critical Review of Major Official Financial-Crisis Inquiry Reports
item.description: Compares the FCIC and major U.K. inquiry reports with primary evidence on investment-bank supervision, housing policy, AIG and Bear Stearns rescue design, and shadow banking, distinguishing legitimate framing critique from unsupported claims of institutional intent.

item.title: Global Population Dynamics: Peaks in Population Level and Growth Rates
item.description: Distinguishes the historical peak in the global population growth rate from the still-projected peak in world population size, using the current UN World Population Prospects 2024 revision and its 2026 interim update.

item.title: The American High Tide: The Postwar Boom and Its Breaking Point, 1945–1975
item.description: The postwar boom was a real and unusually broad high-growth regime, but not the product of one policy or one geopolitical accident. Its strongest explanation is an alignment of rapid productivity growth, rising incomes, transformed household finance, education, bargaining institutions, infrastructure, and international conditions that began to come apart before and during the 1970s.

item.title: The Yankee Leviathan: Grandeur and Self-Indictment in Moby-Dick
item.description: Reads Moby-Dick as a double-action text that magnifies New England and American moral, intellectual, commercial, and political authority while building its own countercase through cosmopolitan labor, democratic federation, epistemic incompletion, anti-imperial property satire, and the destruction of Ahab’s command regime.

item.title: Meme Culture and the “Borderer-Right” Style Hypothesis
item.description: Finds that a low-deference, antagonistic “borderer” meme style is plausible as a measurable construct but cannot be equated with the political right in advance: far-right evidence is substantial in some contexts, while taboo, ridicule, out-group hostility, and irony also occur in left-wing and other meme communities.

item.title: The Borderer Signal: Separating Meme Style from Ideology
item.description: Replaces a circular right-aggression/left-empathy classification with a testable design in which political ideology and meme style are measured independently and the proposed borderer construct must demonstrate reliability, coherence, and cross-context predictive validity to survive.

item.title: The Calculus of the Wire: Oliver Heaviside and the Engineering of Electromagnetism
item.description: A source-audited history of Oliver Heaviside as a mathematical engineer who helped recast Maxwellian field theory, developed distributed transmission-line analysis and the distortionless-line condition, and built an operational calculus for solving circuit and field problems before its mathematical foundations were fully understood.

item.title: The Emptiness of Deleuze
item.description: Tests a polemical critique of Deleuze and finds that the strongest inherited charges misstate his ontology, while a narrower criticism survives: Deleuzian concepts explain genesis, transformation, and capture more readily than they supply normative criteria or institutional designs for legitimate durable political order.

item.title: The Light in the Field: Maxwell, Faraday, and the Making of Electromagnetism
item.description: A source-audited history of how Faraday’s experimental field concepts became Maxwell’s dynamical electromagnetic theory, how Maxwell identified light with electromagnetic propagation, and how later Maxwellians and vector analysis produced the compact four-equation form now taught under Maxwell’s name.

item.title: The World Beneath the War: Material Reality in Westeros and Middle-earth
item.description: Compares material realism in Westeros and Middle-earth using causal integration rather than encyclopedic detail. Martin foregrounds scarcity, logistics, rule, and war while leaving some civilization-wide consequences of multi-year seasons abstract; Tolkien foregrounds landscape, memory, stewardship, and ecological damage without offering a quantitative agronomic simulation.

item.title: Language Under Constraint: A Post-Chomskyan Theory for the LLM Era
item.description: A constructive post-Chomskyan research program that treats language acquisition as constrained learnability rather than a binary contest between innate grammar and statistics. The framework separates learnability, representation, performance, and grounding and requires competing learners to succeed or fail under explicit developmental conditions.

item.title: The Learner in the Corpus: What LLMs Actually Show About Chomsky
item.description: A source-audited assessment of what neural language models actually establish about Chomskyan learnability claims. Specific computational results weaken some poverty-of-the-stimulus and impossible-language arguments, while child-scale data, model inductive bias, harder syntactic phenomena, and cognitive mismatch block a blanket Chomsky refuted verdict.

item.title: Before “Scientific Socialism”: Marx, Engels, and the Communist Manifesto
item.description: A source-audited reconstruction of the relationship between the 1848 Communist Manifesto and the later label “scientific socialism,” separating Marx and Engels’s communist self-designation from Engels’s 1880 codification of the utopian/scientific contrast.

item.title: Proudhon’s Mutualism: Property, Reciprocity, and Mutual Credit
item.description: A source-audited study of Proudhon’s evolving mutualism, from the 1840 critique of absolute property through reciprocal exchange, the 1849 People’s Bank, mature federalism, the later rehabilitation of dispersed property as counter-power, and the divergent French and American mutualist legacies.

item.title: The Unheard Instrument
item.description: A literary but source-disciplined history of the spectral dream behind the Riemann zeros, from the retrospective Hilbert and Pólya anecdotes through Selberg, Montgomery–Dyson, random matrices, Berry–Keating, and Connes, with a strict distinction between evidence for spectral analogy and evidence for an actual Hilbert–Pólya realization.
